To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have developed a new method for the typing of a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in nonamplified DNA, which is applicable in a clinical laboratory, and we have applied this method for the typing and the genotyping of the SNP conferring susceptibility to type-1 diabetes.

we developed a novel approach for the detection of allelic variants in genomic DNA that is based on a time-resolved analysis and that we successfully applied this approach to the detection of the allele conferring the susceptibility to insulin-dependent (type 1) diabetes mellitus.
we have identified the allele conferring the susceptibility to the disease by a F\"orsters resonance energy-transfer-based assay on non-amplified DNA.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the application of the time-resolved F\"orster resonance energy-transfer to the typing of the polymorphic sequences of the DQ beta-chain genes of the human leukocytes antigen system, in order to identify the allelic sequences conferring susceptibility to diabetes mellitus in genomic DNA.
the identification of the DQB*0302 allele of the human leukocite antigen system conferring the susceptibility to the development insulin-dependent diabetes mellittus.
the development of a method for typing the allelic sequences conferring susceptibility to a disease in DNA samples without amplification of the gene region of interest.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the method here proposed, by means of F\"orster resonance energy transfer and time-resolved fluorescence, allows to discriminate, in the absence of PCR, the DNA samples carrying the allele conferring the susceptibility to the development to IDDM from those bearing any other sequence of the DQB region of the human leukocytes antigen system.

the method here proposed, based on the ps-resolved fluorescence of nonamplified DNA, allows the typing of the allelic sequence of the DQB gene conferring susceptibility for IDDM in a sample of human genomic DNA.

the time-resolved FRET method on non-amplified genomic DNA is able to detect, in the presence of the DQB*0302 allele, the DQB1*0302 sequence, which confers susceptibility to the development in humans of insulin-dependent diabetes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the case of the DQB*0302 allele, the time-resolved detection of the donor fluorescence allows the discrimination of the DNA samples containing this allele from those containing any other allelic sequence of the DQB region, in spite of the fact that the donor fluorescence is strongly quenched, and the donor fluorescence decay is very short.

we are able to type the DNA samples for the presence or absence of the allele conferring risk for IDDM, with a detection limit of 1% of the total DNA, and a discrimination limit of 1/2000 for the two alleles.

we have developed and validated a method for the typing of the DQB gene polymorphic sequences, which is able to detect, with a 95% confidence level, the presence of one allele in a DNA sample, even in the absence of any PCR step.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the time-resolved F\"orster-resolved energy-transfer method can be used to discriminate between two different alleles in genomic DNA samples with no PCR amplification.

, by using time-resolved F\"orster-resonant energy transfer, it is possible to type a polymorphic gene by means of a nonamplified DNA sample, with a detection limit of 0.5% of the allele conferring the disease.

the FRET technique is suitable for the analysis of nonamplified DNA samples, and can therefore be exploited in clinical practice for the identification of the alleles of interest in the DQB1 region of the human leukocytes antigen system.
